readings.c3s2:
¶
'''unreasoning''' (un-rē′zn-ing), ''a.'' Not reasoning; not having reasoning faculties; characterized by want of reason.
{{smaller block|To these rational considerations there is superadded, in extreme cases, a panic as ''unreasoning'' as the previous over-confidence.
{{right|''J. S. Mill.''}}}}

'''unreasoningly''' (un-rē′zn-ing-li), ''adv.'' In an unreasoning manner; without reasoning or reflection. ''N. A. Rev.'', CXL. 194.

'''unreave†''' (un-rēv′), ''v. t.'' To take to pieces; disentangle; loose.
{{smaller block|<poem>The worke that she all day did make,
The same at night she did againe ''unreave.''</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', Sonnets, xxiii.}}}}

'''unreaved†''' (un-rēvd′), ''a.'' Not taken or pulled to pieces.
{{smaller block|Could’st thou think that a cottage not too strongly built, and standing so bleak in the very mouth of the winds, could for any long time hold tight and ''unreaved?''
{{right|''Bp. Hall'', Balm of Gilead.}}}}

'''unrebated''' (un-rẹ̄-bā′ted), ''a.'' Same as ''unbated.''
{{smaller block|A number of fencers tried it, with ''unrebated'' swords.
{{right|''Hakewill'', Apology.}}}}

'''unrebukable''' (un-rẹ̄-bū′ka̤-bl), ''a.'' Not deserving rebuke; not obnoxious to censure. 1 Tim. vi. 14. Also spelled ''unrebukeable.''

'''unrecallable''' (un-rẹ̄-kâl′a̤-bl), ''a.'' Not recallable; incapable of being called back, revoked, annulled, or recalled.
{{smaller block|That which is done is ''unrecallable.''
{{right|''Feltham'', Resolves, i. 89.}}}}

'''unrecalling†''' (un-rẹ̄-kâl′ing), ''a.'' Not to be recalled. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>And ever let his ''unrecalling'' crime</poem>}}

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|unquit|6639|unrecognizably}}</noinclude>{{smaller block|'''2.''' Unpaid.
The dai Is past, the dette ''vn-quit.''
{{right|''Holy Rood'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 110.}}}}

'''unquizzable''' (un-kwiz′a̤-bl), ''a.'' [< ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''quiz'' + ''-able.''] Not capable of being quizzed; not open to ridicule.
{{smaller block|Each was dressed out in his No. 1 suit, in most exact and ''unquizzable'' uniform.
{{right|''Marryat'', Frank Mildmay, xv. (''Davies.'')}}}}

'''unraced†''', ''a.'' [ME., < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''raced'', pp. of ''race''<sup>5</sup>.] Unbroken; undestroyed.
{{smaller block|Tho thinges . . . ben kept hoole and ''unraced.''
{{right|''Chaucer'', Boëthius, iv. prose 1.}}}}

'''unracked''' (un-rakt′), ''a.'' Not racked; not having the contents freed from the lees: as, an ''unracked'' vessel. ''Bacon'', Nat. Hist., § 306.

'''unraised''' (un-rāzd′), ''a.'' Not raised. {{smaller|(''a'') Not elevated.}}
{{smaller block|The flat ''unraised'' spirits. ''Shak.'', Hen. V., Prol., l. 9.}}
{{smaller|(''b'') Not abandoned, as a siege.}}
{{smaller block|The siege shulde nat be ''unreysed.''
{{right|''Berners'', tr. of Froissart’s Chron., I. cccxxxviii.}}}}

'''unraked''' (un-rākt′), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not raked: as, land ''unraked.''—'''2.''' Not raked together; not raked up.
{{smaller block|Where fires thou find’st ''unraked.''
{{right|''Shak.'', M. W. of W., v. 5. 48.}}}}

'''3†.''' Not sought or acquired by effort, as by raking.
{{smaller block|He doubtless will command the People to make good his Promises of Maintenance more honourably unask’d, ''unrak’d'' for.
{{right|''Milton'', Touching Hirelings.}}}}

'''unransacked''' (un-ran′sakt), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not ransacked; not searched.—'''2.''' Not pillaged. ''Knolles'', Hist. of the Turks.

'''unraptured''' (un-rap′tṳ̄rd), ''a.'' Not enraptured, enchanted, charmed, or transported.
{{smaller block|Man ''unraptured'', uninflamed.
{{right|''Young'', Night Thoughts, iv.}}}}

'''unravel''' (un-rav′el), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''unraveled'', ''unravelled'', ppr. ''unraveling'', ''unravelling''. [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''ravel''. The prefix is either reversive or intensive, according as ''ravel'' is taken to mean ‘tangle’ or ‘untangle.’] '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To disentangle or separate, as threads; especially, to take out the threads of (textile material). See ''ravel''.
{{smaller block|<poem>I have talked with my own heart,
And have ''unravelled'' my entangled will.</poem>
{{right|''Shelley'', The Cenci, iii. 1.}}
By means of a prism Sir Isaac Newton ''unravelled'' the texture of solar light.
{{right|''Tyndall'', Radiation, § 1.}}}}
'''2.''' To clear from complication or difficulty; unriddle; unfold.
{{smaller block|These, with fifty other points left ''unravelled'', you may endeavor to solve, if you have time.
{{right|''Sterne'', Tristram Shandy, ii. 19.}}
At the first glimpse we see that here there is a mystery to be ''unravelled''.
{{right|''E. A. Freeman'', Venice, p. 74.}}}}
'''3†.''' To separate the connected or united parts of; throw into disorder. {{smaller block|''Unravelling'' all the received principles of reason and religion. {{right|''Tillotson'', Sermons, I. i.}}}}
'''4.''' To unfold or bring to a denouement, as the plot or intrigue of a play. ''Pope.''

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To be unfolded; be disentangled.
{{smaller block|What webs of wonder shall ''unravel'' there!
{{right|''Young'', Night Thoughts, vi.}}}}

'''unraveler, unraveller''' (un-rav′el-ėr), ''n.'' One who or that which unravels.
{{smaller block|Mythologists are indeed very pretty fellows, and are mighty ''unravellers'' of the fables of the old Ethnicks, discovering all the Old Testament concealed in them.
{{right|''T. Brown'', Works, III. 279. (''Davies.'')}}}}

'''unravelment''' (un-rav′el-mẹnt), ''n.'' The act or process of unraveling; disentanglement; unfolding.
{{smaller block|In the course of the ''unravelment'' of the conspiracy against Belle Carlisle we come across many clever touches of character. {{right|''The Academy'', Nov. 15, 1890, p. 447.}}}}

'''unrazored''' (un-rā′zo̤rd), ''a.'' Unshaved.
{{smaller block|Their ''unrazor’d'' lips. {{right|''Milton'', Comus, l. 290.}}}}

'''unreached''' (un-rēcht′), ''a.'' Not reached; not attained to.
{{smaller block|That lofty hill ''unreached.'' {{right|''Dryden.''}}}}

'''unread<sup>1</sup>†''', ''n.'' [ME. ''unred'', ''unræd'', < AS. ''unrǣd'' (= Icel. ''ūrādh'' = Dan. ''uraad''), bad counsel, < ''un-'', not (here ‘bad’), + ''rǣd'', counsel: see ''read'', ''n.''] Bad advice or counsel.

'''unread<sup>2</sup>''' (un-red′), ''a.'' [< ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''read'', pp. of ''read''<sup>1</sup>, ''v.''] '''1.''' Not read; not perused.

{{smaller block|These books are safer and better to be left publickly ''unread.''
{{right|''Hooker'', Eccles. Polity.}}}}

'''2.''' Untaught; not learned in books.
{{smaller block|The clown ''unread'', and half-read gentleman.
{{right|''Dryden'', Hind and Panther, iii. 408.}}}}

'''unreadable''' (un-rē′da-bl), ''a.'' Not readable. {{smaller|(''a'') Incapable of being read or deciphered; illegible: as, ''unreadable'' manuscript or writing. (''b'') Not suitable or fit for reading; not worth reading: as, a dull, ''unreadable'' book or poem.}}
{{smaller block|Goethe . . . wasted his time and thwarted his creative energy on the mechanical mock-antique of an ''unreadable'' “Achilleis.” {{right|''Lowell'', Study Windows, p. 217.}}}}
{{smaller block|Books almost ''unreadable'' to delicate minds. {{right|''Littell’s Living Age'', CLXI. 75.}}}}

'''unreadableness''' (un-rē′da-bl-nes), ''n.'' The quality or state of being unreadable; illegibility. ''Athenæum'', No. 3300, p. 113.

'''unreadily''' (un-red′i-li), ''adv.'' In an unready manner. {{smaller|(''a'') Unpreparedly. (''b'') Not promptly; not quickly. (''c''†) Awkwardly.}}
{{smaller block|Men being first inforced to write their actes and monuments in beasts skinnes dried, in barkes of trees, or otherwise perchance as ''vnreadily''. {{right|''Hakluyt’s Voyages'', II. 171.}}}}

'''unreadiness''' (un-red′i-nes), ''n.'' The character of being unready, in any sense.

'''unready''' (un-red′i), ''a.'' [< ME. ''unredy''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''ready''.] '''1.''' Not ready; not prepared; not fit.
{{smaller block|<poem>A dismal picture of the general doom;
Where souls distracted, when the trumpet blows,
And half ''unready'' with their bodies come.</poem>{{right|''Dryden'', Annus Mirabilis, st. 254.}}}}
'''2.''' Not prompt; not quick.—'''3†.''' Awkward; ungainly.
{{smaller block|An ''unready'' horse, that will neither stop nor turn. {{right|''Bacon'', Youth and Age.}}}}
'''4†.''' Not dressed; undressed.
{{smaller block|<poem>How now, my lords! what, all ''unready'' so?</poem>{{right|''Shak.'', 1 Hen. VI., ii. 1.}}}}

{{smaller block|Enter James, ''unready'', in his night-cap, garterless.
{{right|''Stage Direction in Two Maids of Moreclack.'' (''Nares.'')}}}}

'''To make unready†''', {{smaller|to undress or unharness.}}
{{smaller block|Come, where have you been, wench? ''Make'' me ''unready''. I slept but ill last night. {{right|''Fletcher'', Island Princess, iii.}}

''Make unready'' the horses; thou knowest how.
{{right|''B. Jonson'', New Inn, i. 1.}}}}

'''unready†''' (un-red′i), ''v. t.'' [< ''unready'', ''a.''] To undress.
{{smaller block|Hee remayned with his daughter, to give his wife time of ''unreadying'' herself.
{{right|''Sir P. Sidney'', Arcadia, p. 379. (''Nares.'')}}}}

'''unreal''' (un-rē′ạl), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not real; not substantial; having appearance only; illusive; ideal.
{{smaller block|<poem>Hence, horrible shadow!
''Unreal'' mockery, hence!</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Macbeth, iii. 4. 107.}}}}
'''2.''' Unpractical; visionary.
{{smaller block|Those who have most loudly advertised their passion for seclusion and their intimacy with nature, from Petrarch down, have been mostly sentimentalists, ''unreal'' men. {{right|''Lowell'', Study Windows, p. 205.}}}}
'''Fallacy of unreal middle.''' {{smaller|See ''fallacy''.}}—'''Unreal quantity''', {{smaller|an imaginary quantity.}}

'''unrealism''' (un-rē′ạl-izm), ''n.'' The opposite of realism.

'''unreality''' (un-rẹ̄-al′i̤-ti), ''n.'' '''1.''' Lack of reality or real existence.—'''2.''' That which has no reality or real existence.
{{smaller block|He (Julius Cæsar) was too sincere to stoop to ''unreality''. He held to the facts of this life and to his own convictions. {{right|''Froude'', Cæsar, p. 549.}}}}
'''3.''' Unpractical character; visionariness.

{{smaller block|The ''unreality'' of the optimistic religions of the day was what he attacked unceasingly from youth to age, with an energy as honest in its way as Carlyle’s.
{{right|''The Critic'', XIV. 243.}}}}

'''unrealize''' (un-rē′al-īz), ''v. t.'' [< ''unreal'' + ''-ize''.] To take away the reality of; make or consider unreal; divest of reality; present or treat in an ideal form. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|The men, the women, . . . the lounger, the beggar, the boys, the dogs, are ''unrealized'' at once.
{{right|''Emerson'', Miscellanies, p. 47.}}}}

'''unreason''' (un-rē′zn), ''n.'' Lack of reason; unreasonableness; irrationality; nonsense; folly; absurdity.—'''Abbot of unreason.''' {{smaller|See ''abbot''.}}

'''unreason†''' (un-rē′zn), ''v. t.'' [< ''unreason'', ''n.''] To prove to be unreasonable; disprove by argument. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|To ''unreason'' the equity of God’s proceedings. {{right|''South.''}}}}

'''unreasonable''' (un-rē′zn-a̤-bl), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not reasonable or agreeable to reason; irrational.
{{smaller block|For it is an ''vnresonable'' religioun that hath riȝte nouȝte of certeyne. {{right|''Piers Plowman'' (B), vi. 153.}}
If he [Henry VIII.] seems to act upon pure self-will, he is able to give a reason for his acts, and that such a reason as we cannot on mere prejudice determine to be ''unreasonable.'' {{right|''Stubbs'', Medieval and Modern Hist., p. 244.}}}}
'''2.''' Exceeding the bounds of reason; beyond what is reasonable or moderate; exorbitant; immoderate: as, an ''unreasonable'' price.
{{smaller block|The pretence was infinitely ''unreasonable,'' and therefore had the fate of senseless allegations, it disbanded presently. {{right|''Jer. Taylor'', Works (ed. 1835), I. 77.}}}}

{{smaller block|An alarmist by nature, an aristocrat by party, he [Xenophon] carried to an ''unreasonable'' excess his horror of popular turbulence. {{right|''Macaulay'', History.}}}}
'''3†.''' Not endowed with reason; irrational.
{{smaller block|The nature of creatures ''unreasonable.''
{{right|''Sir T. Elyot'', The Governour, iii. 3.}}
''Unreasonable'' creatures feed their young.
{{right|''Shak.'', 3 Hen. VI., ii. 2. 26.}}}}
'''4.''' Not listening to or acting according to reason; not guided by reason; not influenced by reason.
{{smaller block|I must be most ''unreasonable'' to be dissatisfied at any thing that he chooses to put in a book which I never shall read. {{right|''Trevelyan'', in Life of Macaulay, I. 204.}}}}
'''5†.''' Inconvenient.
{{smaller block|We departed to our lodging, desiring to know whether our coming the next day might not be uneasy or ''unreasonable'' to her. {{right|''Penn'', Travels in Holland, etc.}}}}
{{smaller|='''Syn.''' ''Absurd, Silly, Foolish'', etc. (see ''absurd''), obstinate, wrong-headed, extravagant, unfair, unjust, extortionate.}}

'''unreasonableness''' (un-rē′zn-a̤-bl-nes), ''n.'' The state or character of being unreasonable, in any sense.

'''unreasonably''' (un-rē′zn-a̤-bli), ''adv.'' In an unreasonable manner; contrary to reason; foolishly; excessively; immoderately.

'''unreasoned''' (un-rē′znd), ''a.'' Not reasoned or argued; not due to reason or reasoning; not founded on reason; not thought out.
{{smaller block|Old prejudices and ''unreasoned'' habits.
{{right|''Burke'', Rev. in France.}}
The ''unreasoned'' denial of a fact is quite as illogical as its blind acceptance. {{right|''Nineteenth Century'', XXIV. 586.}}}}

'''unreasoning''' (un-rē′zn-ing), ''a.'' Not reasoning; not having reasoning faculties; characterized by want of reason.
{{smaller block|To these rational considerations there is superadded, in extreme cases, a panic as ''unreasoning'' as the previous over-confidence.
{{right|''J. S. Mill.''}}}}

'''unreasoningly''' (un-rē′zn-ing-li), ''adv.'' In an unreasoning manner; without reasoning or reflection. ''N. A. Rev.'', CXL. 194.

'''unreave†''' (un-rēv′), ''v. t.'' To take to pieces; disentangle; loose.
{{smaller block|<poem>The worke that she all day did make,
The same at night she did againe ''unreave.''</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', Sonnets, xxiii.}}}}

'''unreaved†''' (un-rēvd′), ''a.'' Not taken or pulled to pieces.
{{smaller block|Could’st thou think that a cottage not too strongly built, and standing so bleak in the very mouth of the winds, could for any long time hold tight and ''unreaved?''
{{right|''Bp. Hall'', Balm of Gilead.}}}}

'''unrebated''' (un-rẹ̄-bā′ted), ''a.'' Same as ''unbated.''
{{smaller block|A number of fencers tried it, with ''unrebated'' swords.
{{right|''Hakewill'', Apology.}}}}

'''unrebukable''' (un-rẹ̄-bū′ka̤-bl), ''a.'' Not deserving rebuke; not obnoxious to censure. 1 Tim. vi. 14. Also spelled ''unrebukeable.''

'''unrecallable''' (un-rẹ̄-kâl′a̤-bl), ''a.'' Not recallable; incapable of being called back, revoked, annulled, or recalled.
{{smaller block|That which is done is ''unrecallable.''
{{right|''Feltham'', Resolves, i. 89.}}}}

'''unrecalling†''' (un-rẹ̄-kâl′ing), ''a.'' Not to be recalled. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>And ever let his ''unrecalling'' crime</poem> Have time to wail th’ abusing of his time.
{{right|''Shak.'', Lucrece, l. 993.}}}}

'''unreceived''' (un-rē-sēvd′), ''a.'' Not received; not taken; not come into possession; not embraced or adopted. ''Hooker'', Eccles. Polity, v. § 54.

'''unreckonable''' (un-rek′n-a̤-bl), ''a.'' Not capable of being reckoned or counted; immeasurable; immense. ''Hawthorne'', Seven Gables, ii.

'''unreckoned''' (un-rek′nd), ''a.'' Not reckoned, computed, counted, or summed up. ''Dryden'', Don Sebastian, iii. 1.

'''unreclaimable''' (un-rẹ̄-klā′ma̤-bl), ''a.'' Irreclaimable. ''Bp. Hall'', Sermons, 2 Pet. i. 10.

'''unreclaimably''' (un-rẹ̄-klā′ma̤-bli), ''adv.'' Irreclaimably. ''Bp. Hall'', Peace-Maker, § 8.

'''unreclaimed''' (un-rẹ̄-klāmd′), ''a.'' Not reclaimed. {{smaller|(''a'') Not brought to a domestic state; not tamed.}}
{{smaller block|A savageness in ''unreclaimed'' blood.
{{right|''Shak.'', Hamlet, ii. 1. 34.}}
Bullocks ''unreclaimed'' to bear the yoke.
{{right|''Dryden'', tr. of Ovid’s Metamorph., xiii.}}}}
{{smaller|(''b'') Not reformed; not called back from vice to virtue: as, a sinner ''unreclaimed.'' (''c'') Not brought into a state of cultivation, as desert or wild land.}}

'''unrecognizable''' (un-rek′ọg-nī-za̤-bl), ''a.'' Not recognizable; incapable of being recognized; irrecognizable. ''Coleridge.''

'''unrecognizably''' (un-rek′ọg-nī-za̤-bli), ''adv.'' In an unrecognizable manner; without or beyond recognition.<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
